feedback: If a child says only birds lay eggs: sort more animals together — many fish, frogs, lizards and insects lay eggs too; eggs are not just a bird thing.
If a child says a dog, cat or human lays eggs: contrast these live-birth mammals with the egg-layers using familiar examples.
When the platypus lays an egg or the shark bears live young, treat the giggle/surprise as the point: nature has exceptions, keep these as curiosities rather than rules to master.
Reinforce correct sorts by naming the group: 'Yes — the frog lays eggs in a pond; the cow has a live calf.'
activities.intendedInsight: Many kinds of animals lay eggs — not just birds — and most mammals have live young; nature also has surprising exceptions, so the shortcut 'mammals are born, everything else lays eggs' doesn't always hold.
learnerActions: Place or group animal pictures into two bins: EGG-LAYERS and LIVE-YOUNG.
Put the hen, an egg-laying fish (e.g. a salmon or goldfish), frog, an egg-laying lizard (e.g. a gecko) and a beetle into the egg-layers bin; put the dog, cow, whale and human into the live-young bin.
After sorting with familiar animals, meet a surprise: a platypus (a mammal that LAYS eggs) and a shark that bears LIVE young — discuss why these are delightful exceptions, not new rules to memorise.
Say aloud one animal that lays eggs and one animal that has live babies.
activities.title: Sort the animals: egg-layers or live-young?

feedback: If a child calls the tadpole a different animal or a fish: walk through the sequence egg→tadpole→froglet→frog — it is one animal changing shape as it grows, not a new animal.
If a child expects every baby to look like its parent: contrast the lamb→sheep (same) pairing with the tadpole→frog (different) pairing so both patterns are held together.
Name the surprise when the frog or butterfly emerges — the moment one creature becomes something so different is a memorable anchor.
activities.intendedInsight: A tadpole IS a baby frog and a caterpillar IS a baby butterfly — the SAME animal at an early life stage. Some young change shape completely as they grow (metamorphosis) while others look like small versions of their parents from early on.
learnerActions: Advance a life-cycle sequence step by step: spawn → tadpole → froglet → frog, watching legs sprout and the tail shrink.
Advance a second sequence: egg → caterpillar → chrysalis → butterfly, watching the caterpillar eat, change into a chrysalis, and emerge as a butterfly.
After each transformation, decide and tag whether the grown-up 'looks the same' or 'looks different' from its baby.
Compare with a 'mini-adult' pairing: place a lamb beside a sheep and a chick beside a hen — these already look like small versions of their parents.
activities.title: Grow the baby: watch a creature transform

feedback: Target answer for the frog prompt: the tadpoles ARE baby frogs — the same animal at an early stage. As they grow they change (metamorphosis): they grow legs, lose the tail, and become frogs. They are not a different kind of animal and not fish.
If a child treats different-looking young as separate animals, this shows only partial understanding — return to the 'grow the baby' sequence to show it is one animal changing.
The 'what will happen as they grow' part is the key tell: a child who accepts that some young change form will predict the change rather than call the tadpole a fish.
activities.intendedInsight: Children can give examples of egg-layers and live-bearers, and recognise that a very different-looking baby (tadpole, caterpillar) is still the same animal, which will change as it grows.
learnerActions: Match each baby to its grown-up (baby→adult pairing).
Put life-stage cards in the right order (e.g. order the tadpole→frog stages).
Categorise a fresh set of animals as egg-layers or live-young.

Answer the diagnostic prompt: 'A frog lays eggs in a pond, and out come tadpoles that look nothing like frogs. Are the tadpoles baby frogs, or a completely different animal? How do you know — and what will happen to them as they grow?'
Discuss: Does a kitten look like a small cat or completely different? Do ALL babies look like their parents? What will grow on the tadpole, and what will disappear, as it gets bigger?
activities.title: Check and talk: same animal or different?
